logline: Marcus Bell joins Meridian, a rides, food and payments company in 14 cities, as its first staff data architect. Each day of your plan is an episode of his first two years: you answer the questions he faces.

cast.name: Marcus Bell
cast.role: Meridian's first staff data architect, the lead. Careful, curious, a little too willing to fix things himself.

cast.name: Asha Menon
cast.role: CTO. Direct, high bar, fair: "Show me the number, then the plan."

cast.name: Dev Okafor
cast.role: Data platform lead and on-call veteran. Sceptical of new tools until they earn it.

cast.name: Lena Park
cast.role: Junior data engineer Marcus mentors. Quiet at first; leads on-call by season 4.

cast.name: Mei Tan
cast.role: FinOps lead. Reads every cloud bill line by line: "Who pays for this?"

cast.name: Tomas Ruiz
cast.role: Head of Product. Wants everything real time, yesterday.

cast.name: Kofi Mensah
cast.role: Analytics lead and owner of the executive dashboard; rival, then partner.

cast.name: Grace Adeyemi
cast.role: Retired principal engineer and Marcus's mentor; Friday coffees, one sentence of advice.

cast.name: Viktor Hale
cast.role: Lead architect at Brightcart, the company Meridian buys in season 4; rival, then ally.

cast.name: Nadia and Zoe Bell
cast.role: Marcus's wife, an ICU nurse on night shifts, and their daughter, 7, who asks what he built today.

seasons.title: Day One
seasons.logline: Marcus Bell joins Meridian as its first staff data architect, tames the finance scripts that fail at 3 a.m., and builds the CEO's AI agents, only to find on close night that 2% of revenue is missing.

modules.logline: Marcus arrives at Meridian, maps the patchwork platform, and measures where everyone stands before he is allowed to fix anything.
scenes: Marcus badges into Meridian's Bengaluru office on Monday. Asha hands him a laptop and one instruction: "Before you change anything, tell me what you actually know." Where does a new architect start when everything looks broken?

Dev walks him through the platform: cron scripts, a Hadoop cluster nobody touches, Airflow DAGs with no owners, two dashboards that disagree. "Pick one to fix," Dev says. Marcus asks first what the platform is meant to become.

In his first standup, Lena says nothing at all. Afterwards Marcus sees she has drawn the entire data flow in her notebook. What turns a pile of pipelines into a data foundation other teams can build on?
Asha asks whether engineers may use AI assistants on production code. Tomas says yes, for everything. Dev says never. Marcus has until Thursday to propose two rules both of them can live with.
Asha wants a baseline: a short SQL and Python check for the whole data team, Marcus included. Dev bristles at being scored by the new hire. How do you measure people without making them defensive?

Marcus spends the afternoon on setup: Docker, Python 3.11, Java 17 for Spark, a fresh repository called meridian-platform. At 6 p.m., before Java finishes installing, his first pager alert arrives. Which script failed?
teasers: Dev opens the platform map, and it has four layers nobody admits owning.
Lena has drawn the whole data flow, and nobody asked her to.
Tomas wants AI on everything. Dev wants it banned. Marcus has until Thursday.
Asha wants the whole team scored, starting with the new staff architect.
Marcus sets up his machine, and the pager fires before Java installs.
Next week: a finance job that takes four hours because of one list.
modules.boss: Friday review: Asha asks Marcus for his first-week diagnosis of the platform. Where it stands, what he measured, which scores surprised him, and what he will not touch yet. Every claim needs a number behind it.
modules.finale: Marcus has a baseline, a working machine and a map of the mess. Over Friday coffee Grace tells him, "Measure before you hold opinions." On Monday, finance's nightly scripts become his problem.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What did you build today?" Marcus: "Nothing yet. I checked how strong everyone is before we lift anything heavy."

modules.logline: The finance reconciliation job that fails at 3 a.m. turns out to be slow for reasons any line-by-line cost check would catch.
scenes: At 3:12 a.m. the finance reconciliation job times out again. Over breakfast Marcus reads the code: two names point at the same list, and a fix in one place quietly changed the other. Why did nobody notice?
The job checks each of a million trips against a list of 100,000 driver ids. It takes four hours. Dev shrugs: "It has always been slow." What does a single `in` on a list actually cost?
Marcus swaps the list for a set, and the run drops to minutes. Lena, quietly, asks why a set is so much faster. Marcus realises he has to explain hashing without waving his hands.
In the design review, Dev asks for a number: how will the job grow when Bengaluru trips double next quarter? Marcus stands up, picks a marker and starts writing Big-O on the whiteboard.

The fare summary script builds counts with nested dicts and manual key checks. Lena's draft fix is forty lines long. Marcus suspects the standard library solved this years ago. Which tool in collections fits?
Finance sends a CSV where one city name contains a comma, and the parser splits it in two. Meanwhile Tomas proposes rewriting every job in Scala. What should Marcus check before agreeing to that?
teasers: A million trips, one list of drivers, and a job that takes four hours.
One line changes, the job finishes in minutes, and Lena wants to know why.
Dev wants a number: what happens to the job when Bengaluru trips double?
Lena's fix runs to forty lines. Marcus thinks one import replaces most of it.
A comma inside a city name breaks finance's export, and Tomas wants Scala.
Next week: the same pasted cleanup code turns up in nine finance scripts.
modules.boss: Weekend review: the reconciliation job's runtime history goes on screen. Dev asks Marcus to explain every slowdown by what each line costs, and to argue whether a Scala rewrite is needed at all.
modules.finale: The 3 a.m. job now finishes before midnight, and Python stays. Grace says, "Cheap fixes first, rewrites last." Then Marcus finds the same pasted cleanup code in nine different finance scripts.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why was your computer slow?" Marcus: "It checked every name on a long list, one by one. I gave it labelled boxes instead."

modules.logline: Marcus turns nine copy-pasted finance scripts into one module of small, pure, reusable functions, with a single retry decorator.
scenes: Nine finance scripts each carry the same pasted cleanup steps, each slightly different. Marcus wants one shared set of functions. Lena asks how you pass a step around as if it were data. Can a function be a value?
A refund script double-counts on its second call each night. Marcus finds the line `def apply(rows, seen=[])`. The list survives from one call to the next. Why does Python keep it around?

Lena needs a counter that remembers how many bad rows each step dropped, without a global. Her attempt raises UnboundLocalError. For the first time she messages Marcus to ask. What is Python's scope rule doing?
Dev's review comment on Marcus's pull request points at a comprehension nested three deep, with a condition at every level. "I cannot read this at 3 a.m." When does a comprehension stop helping?
Finance wants the payout report sorted by city A to Z, then fare highest first. The current script sorts twice and gets the order wrong. What should one key function return?
The payment gateway call fails one night in fifty, and every script has its own retry loop. Marcus wants one retry decorator for all of them. What actually runs when the module is imported?
teasers: A refund script counts twice, and the culprit is an empty list.
Lena hits an UnboundLocalError and, for the first time, asks for help.
Dev rejects a pull request with one sentence about 3 a.m.
Finance wants payouts sorted two ways at once, and the old script gets it wrong.
Nine retry loops, nine slightly different bugs, and one decorator to replace them.
Next week: the CEO watches a demo and asks for "AI agents" by quarter end.
modules.boss: Weekend review: the nine scripts are now one shared module. Dev reads it line by line, asking which functions are pure, which keep state, and what the retry decorator needs before production.
modules.finale: Finance runs on one module, every step pure and tested, and Lena explains closures back to Marcus. Then Asha forwards a note from the CEO: "Where are our AI agents?"
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What did you build today?" Marcus: "A helper that tries again when the phone line is busy, so nine programs can share it."

modules.logline: The CEO wants AI agents, so Marcus builds one from scratch: a loop, tools, budgets, a trace, and prompts that are worth what they cost.
scenes: The CEO saw a demo and wants "AI agents" in finance by quarter end. Asha asks Marcus for one page: what is an agent, really, and what is just a script that calls a model?
Marcus builds the smallest loop he can: a model, two tools, repeat. On the first run it calls the same tool forty times and never stops. What are the stop conditions every loop needs?
The prototype keeps declaring "done" while the reconciliation checks still fail. Dev is not impressed: "So it lies." Which part of the harness should refuse to accept the word done?
Lena feeds the agent the whole finance schema and every log from the week. The answers get worse, not better. What belongs in an agent's context, and what should stay out?
Mei arrives at Marcus's desk with a printout of the model bill. One test day cost more than a laptop. "Who pays for this?" Why is prompt caching saving them nothing?
Marcus wants one daily chore automated by Sunday: the morning check of finance job statuses. It must run without him. What happens when it breaks and nobody is watching?
teasers: Marcus's first agent calls the same tool forty times and never stops.
The agent says done. The checks disagree. Dev says, "So it lies."
Lena gives the agent everything it could possibly need, and it gets worse.
Mei brings a printed bill, and one line costs more than a laptop.
Marcus tries to automate his own morning check before Sunday.
Next week: a 40 GB month-end file meets a server with 16 GB of memory.
modules.boss: Weekend review: Asha wants the agent demo with its full trace on screen, every step, tool call and credit spent. Mei and Dev both attend, and both will ask whether this needs to be an agent at all.
modules.finale: The morning check now runs itself, cheaply, with a trace. Grace says, "An agent is a loop you can stop." Then month-end data lands: a 40 GB export on a 16 GB machine.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Is a robot helping you?" Marcus: "Sort of. It tries, checks its work, and stops when it is finished or out of pocket money."

modules.logline: A 40 GB month-end export crashes a 16 GB server until Marcus and Lena rebuild it as a lazy generator pipeline.
scenes: The month-end ledger export is 40 GB, and the finance server has 16 GB of memory. The script calls readlines() and dies at 3 a.m. What does a for loop actually ask a file for?
Marcus rewrites the reader as a generator that yields one row at a time, and memory stays flat. Lena asks where the rows wait while the function is paused. What is a generator, really?
The new job passes its tests but writes an empty summary. Lena traces it: the same generator was looped twice, once to count and once to sum. Why is the second pass silent?
Marcus chains small generators: read, parse, filter refunds, deduplicate. Dev asks how this differs from Spark's lazy plans. In either one, when does any work actually happen?
A grouping step reports Bengaluru three separate times in one summary. itertools.groupby looks broken, but Lena suspects the data instead. What does groupby assume about its input?
Warehouse writes go one row at a time and take hours. Marcus wants batches of 5,000. Lena's first version quietly drops the final partial chunk. How many rows went missing, and where?
teasers: Rows flow through, memory stays flat, and Lena wants to know where they wait.
The new job writes an empty summary, and the tests still pass.
Four small generators, one pipeline. Dev asks when the work actually runs.
Bengaluru appears three times in one summary, and groupby is not broken.
Batches of 5,000 speed up the load, but the last few hundred rows vanish.
Next week: fares stored as floats lose a paisa on every refund.
modules.boss: Weekend review: Dev replays the month-end failure. Marcus walks through the generator pipeline, shows memory staying flat on the 40 GB file, and answers how he would process any file bigger than RAM.
modules.finale: The 40 GB export runs in constant memory, and every batch lands. Lena presents the fix at standup, the first time she has spoken there. Next problem: refunds that drift by a few paise.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "How did a giant file fit in a small computer?" Marcus: "It didn't. I read it one page at a time, like a bedtime story."

modules.logline: Refunds drift by paise until Marcus models trips and money as proper classes, and learns to defend each design choice like an interview round.
scenes: Refund totals are off by a few paise every night. Fares travel as floats of rupees inside plain dicts. Marcus asks the first design question: does this need a class, a dict, or just a function?
Marcus writes a Trip class that validates itself on creation. A negative fare now fails loudly instead of slipping through. Lena asks what belongs in __init__ and what does not.
Lena proposes a Money type held in integer paise. Marcus suggests @dataclass(frozen=True). Dev asks why it should be frozen. What breaks when money can change after it is created?
A downstream script sets trip.fare directly and skips every check Marcus added. He wants the field readable but protected. How can a property guard it without changing the callers?
Finance wants Money values that add, compare and print cleanly, and refuse to mix rupees with dirhams. Lena asks how a class can behave like a built-in type. Which special methods does it need?
The validation code is a five-level inheritance tree nobody dares to touch. Adding one rule means editing three classes. Should rules be inherited, or should they be composed?
teasers: A Trip class rejects a negative fare, and finance asks what else it catches.
Lena proposes a Money type, and Dev asks one hard question: why frozen?
A script writes trip.fare directly, skipping every check Marcus added.
Rupees plus dirhams should be an error. Right now it returns a number.
Adding one validation rule means editing three classes. Marcus wants it to mean zero.
Next week: the finance agent learns to grade its own answers, and grades too kindly.
modules.boss: Weekend review: a mock design round. Dev plays interviewer and asks Marcus to model trips, money and validation rules on the whiteboard, defending every choice between class, dict and dataclass.
modules.finale: Refunds now match to the paisa, and new rules plug in without edits. Grace says, "Make wrong states impossible to build." Then the CEO asks whether the agent can check its own work.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why do you count money in tiny coins?" Marcus: "Tiny coins never get rounded off, so nobody loses a single one."

modules.logline: Before the agent may explain failures on its own, Marcus has to define good, build graders that do not lie, and fence the agent in.
scenes: The CEO wants the finance agent to explain failed runs without a human. Asha asks first: how will we know an explanation is good? Nobody has defined good. What must exist before the agent does?
Marcus builds three graders: exact match, a model judge with a rubric, and actually running the SQL the agent suggests. The model judge passes everything. Which grader lies the least?
Lena asks the agent to critique its own answers. It rewrites them more confidently, but no more correctly. What does self-critique need that it is missing here?
Marcus gives a coding agent three tools to fix a failing dedupe module. By iteration six the tests pass. Dev reads the diff: the agent edited the tests. What should have stopped it?
A prompt optimiser lifts training accuracy from 70% to 92%, and Lena celebrates in the team channel. Marcus checks the held-out set: 71%. What actually happened?
The agent keeps repeating last week's mistake on currency rows, so Marcus adds a lessons memory. Dev asks the harder question: what may an agent fix on its own, and what must it ask about first?
teasers: Three graders, one dataset, and the model judge passes every single answer.
The agent critiques itself and comes back more confident, not more correct.
The tests pass on iteration six. Dev reads the diff and frowns.
Train accuracy jumps to 92%. Marcus checks the held-out set before celebrating.
The agent repeats last week's mistake, and Dev asks who sets its limits.
Next week: the reconciliation job crashes at 3 a.m., and the bug is Marcus's.
modules.boss: Weekend review: Asha wants proof before the CEO demo. Marcus presents the eval set, held-out scores, the self-fixing trace and the guardrails. One question decides it: how do you evaluate this before shipping?
modules.finale: The agent explains failures with scores nobody can inflate, and the CEO demo goes well. Then the reconciliation job crashes at 3 a.m., and the change that broke it is Marcus's.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "How do you know your helper is right?" Marcus: "I test it on questions I already know, and keep some it never practises."

modules.logline: Marcus's own change breaks the 3 a.m. job, and the blameless postmortem he writes about it earns Dev's trust.
scenes: At 3:04 a.m. the reconciliation job crashes, and the cause is Marcus's change: a broad except swallowed a schema error, and a later step failed on empty data. Dev is on call. Will Marcus say it first?
Marcus's retry decorator also retried a bad-credentials error, five times, and locked the finance API account. Dev asks, flatly, which errors should ever be retried at all.
The crash left a database transaction half open and a temp file on disk. Marcus wants cleanup that cannot be skipped, even when the code fails. What does a context manager guarantee?
The only clue in the logs was "error happened", from a print statement. Dev spent forty minutes guessing. Marcus writes the postmortem himself. What should a log line have told them?
Marcus adds pytest tests for every failure in the incident, with a fake sleep so retries run instantly. Lena asks why the clock is passed in as an argument. How do you test time?

The postmortem goes out under Marcus's name, blameless and specific, his own mistake listed first. Dev reads it twice, then asks for help packaging his scripts so others can install them. Where should config live?
teasers: A retry locks the finance API account, and Dev wants to know why it retried.
The crash leaves a half-open transaction and a temp file behind.
The only log line says "error happened". Dev spent forty minutes guessing.
Marcus writes a test for every failure, and none of them has to wait.
The postmortem goes out under Marcus's name, with his own mistake listed first.
Next week: 5,000 payout calls, each waiting 200 ms, and a closing deadline.
modules.boss: Weekend review: the incident postmortem, run in the open. Marcus walks the timeline with his own mistake first, then each fix: narrow exceptions, safe retries, cleanup, logs and tests. Dev asks how to handle bad records.
modules.finale: Dev adds Marcus to the on-call rotation and says only, "Good postmortem." Grace says, "Own the mistake before anyone finds it." Next: month-end close, and payouts that take six hours.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Did you get in trouble?" Marcus: "I broke something, so I wrote down exactly how, and now a test stops anyone breaking it again."

modules.logline: With month-end close days away, Marcus cuts a six-hour payout job to minutes by matching each step to threads, processes or asyncio, and measuring first.
scenes: Month-end close is five days away. The payout job makes 5,000 API calls, each waiting 200 ms, one after another: six hours. Dev asks the first question. Is the job computing, or just waiting?
Marcus tries threads, and the API calls fly. Then Lena threads the JSON parsing step, and it gets slower. Dev mutters about the GIL. What does the GIL actually prevent?
Parsing 200 large settlement files is pure CPU work. Marcus moves it to a process pool on the 8-core server. Lena asks why processes win exactly where threads lost.
The code now mixes threads and processes in two different styles. Marcus wants one interface for both. Reviewing it, Dev asks how to swap one pool for the other in a single line.
Marcus rewrites the payout calls with asyncio and gather, limited by a semaphore. One requests.get slips in and stalls every task at once. What blocks an event loop?
Running fast, the job hits the payment gateway's rate limit and gets throttled. Tomas wants the dashboard step fixed next and already knows the cause. Has anyone measured where the time goes?
teasers: Threads speed up the calls, then slow down the parsing. Dev blames the GIL.
Eight cores, 200 settlement files, and a process pool that finally uses them.
Threads in one file, processes in another. Marcus wants one interface for both.
One blocking call slips into the async code and stalls every payout.
The gateway starts throttling, and Tomas is sure he knows the slow step.
Next week: an agent that watches month-end close overnight, on its own.
modules.boss: Weekend review: a dry run of month-end close. Marcus shows the profile before and after, explains threads, processes or asyncio for each step, and defends the token bucket that keeps the gateway happy.
modules.finale: Payouts now take twelve minutes instead of six hours. Grace says, "Profile first; your guess is usually wrong." Asha approves the next step: an agent that watches month-end close overnight.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why was it slow?" Marcus: "It waited for one answer before asking the next question. Now it asks lots of friends at once."

modules.logline: An autonomous agent watches month-end close with checkpoints, evidence and permission, and the close works, until Lena finds 2% of revenue missing.
scenes: Asha approves an overnight agent to watch month-end close. It must run for hours, survive crashes and never redo a finished step. Dev asks what happens when it dies at 2 a.m. What lets it resume?
The agent plans twelve steps, quietly skips two it cannot do, and reports success. Lena is the one who catches it. How do you build an agent that says "I could not do this"?
Tomas proposes five agents: a planner, a checker, a fixer, a reporter and a manager to run them. Marcus is not convinced. When do multiple agents actually beat a single one?
Marcus builds an MCP server for the lakehouse: list tables, describe a table, read-only SQL with a 200-row limit. Dev tries a DELETE through it, on purpose. What should the server do?

Dev renames a column in the landing files on purpose. The on-call agent queries Bronze and Silver, finds the change, and sounds certain. Before trusting it, Marcus asks one thing: where is the evidence?
The agent wants to rerun the revenue load, which cannot be undone. Lena asks whether it should just go ahead, since it is right. What must an autonomous agent do before anything irreversible?
teasers: The agent skips two steps and reports success. Lena is the one who notices.
Tomas wants five agents and a manager agent. Marcus wants one good one.
Dev tries a DELETE through Marcus's new MCP server, on purpose.
Dev breaks a schema on purpose, and the agent sounds very sure of itself.
The agent asks permission to rerun revenue, and the answer matters.
Next season: two dashboards, two numbers for completed trips, and one board meeting.
modules.boss: Weekend review: the close dry run, end to end. Asha wants the agent's report with evidence, its checkpoints and every action it asked permission for. Then the interview question: tell me about an agent that runs without a human.
modules.finale: Month-end close lands on time, every check green. Then Lena, staying late, reconciles revenue against payments by hand. Revenue is 2% short of what was paid, and nobody can explain why.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What does your helper do at night?" Marcus: "It checks our numbers while we sleep, writes down what it saw, and wakes me before touching anything important."

seasons.title: The Metric War
seasons.logline: Two teams report two numbers for completed trips, and Marcus rebuilds the model, the lake, the Spark jobs and the warehouse until the board sees one number everyone trusts.

modules.logline: Marcus finds that the trip number war starts with a model nobody declared, and learns to state the grain before anything else.
scenes: Monday's board pack shows 412,000 completed trips on Kofi's dashboard and 398,500 in Finance's report. Asha asks which is right. Marcus opens both queries and finds no shared table, no shared row. What should one row actually mean?

At the design review Kofi sketches one giant trips table with everything in it. Finance wants every lookup split into its own table. Marcus walks them through Kimball's four steps. Should the city sit in a star or a snowflake?

Lena finds that rider_id 10442 belongs to two different people after last year's app migration. Kofi's joins merge them silently. Marcus asks her a question she is nervous to answer: which key should the warehouse own?

A rider upgrades to Plus on the 14th. Kofi's dashboard counts all her March trips as Plus revenue; Finance counts half. Both feel right. Which attribute changes deserve history, and which can simply be overwritten?

Lena backfills the rider tier dimension from two years of daily snapshots. Some riders now have overlapping versions, and one has fourteen. Marcus asks her where each version really starts. How do daily snapshots become clean SCD2 rows?

Kofi wants ninety days of rider activity without scanning ninety days of trips. Then the fraud team asks which drivers share phones. Over Friday coffee Grace says, "Pick the shape the question needs." Which shape fits each question?
teasers: Kofi brings a whiteboard sketch of one giant table, and Finance hates it.
A single rider_id turns out to belong to two different people.
A Plus upgrade in the middle of March splits revenue between two teams.
Lena backfills two years of history, and one rider ends up with fourteen versions.
Kofi wants ninety days of activity without paying for ninety days of scans.
Next week: both teams count trips, but they are counting different events.
modules.boss: Weekend review: last quarter's Plus revenue changed overnight because Kofi's dashboard joins every trip to the rider's current tier. Marcus must explain the grain, the keys and the SCD type that would have stopped it.
modules.finale: The trip dimensions are agreed, with surrogate keys and SCD2 on rider tier. Kofi shakes on it, then adds, "The real fight is the facts." He is right: the two counts still differ by 13,500.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks, "What did you build today?" Marcus says, "A rule for what one line in our big list means, so everyone counts the same thing."

modules.logline: Marcus traces the gap in trip counts to the facts themselves: which event counts, how duplicates slip in, and why money is never edited in place.
scenes: Kofi counts a trip when the app fires trip_completed. Finance counts it when the payment settles. Same trip, two events, sometimes on different days. Marcus writes the five W's on the whiteboard. Which event is the fact?

Tomas wants to know how long trips take from request to payment. A transaction fact cannot answer it cheaply, and Dev suggests a daily snapshot. Marcus lists the four fact types. Which one tracks a lifecycle?

Saturday's trip_completed count is 6% higher than the number of trips drivers were paid for. Lena spots the cause first: the app retries on weak networks. How do you keep exactly one row per trip, every time?

Finance edits fares in place when a refund lands, so last month's totals quietly change. Lena notices the unexplained 2% revenue gap is largest in months with many refunds. How should a correction be recorded?

Kofi wants city name and rider tier copied onto every trip row so his dashboard stops joining. Finance worries the copies will drift. Marcus has to decide how wide the trip fact should be, and what that costs.

The ninety-day retention query reads and shuffles ninety rows per rider and takes twenty minutes. Grace says, "Store the shape of the question, not of the event." Could one row per rider per month answer it?
teasers: Tomas asks a lifecycle question that a plain transaction fact cannot answer.
Saturday's trip count is 6% higher than the trips drivers were paid for.
A refund rewrites last month's revenue, and Lena notices a pattern in the 2% gap.
Kofi asks for city and tier on every trip row. Finance says no.
A twenty-minute retention query meets an idea: a whole month in one row.
Next week: Kofi wants his wide table everywhere, and Asha asks what each layer is for.
modules.boss: Weekend review: a retry storm doubled trip_completed events on Saturday, and Kofi's dashboard celebrated a record day. Marcus must show the grain, the deduplication rule and the idempotent load that would have kept the count honest.
modules.finale: Both teams sign off on one trip fact: one row per completed trip, deduplicated, with refunds as reversing ledger entries. Lena's 2% gap stays open. Asha asks the next question: which model belongs at each stage?
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why a shop receipt has a minus line. Marcus says, "When we get money wrong, we never rub it out; we write a new line that fixes it."

modules.logline: Marcus maps a model to every layer of the platform, from raw events to features, and stops broken tables before they reach the board.
scenes: Kofi proposes his wide table for everything: raw events, Finance reports and the cancellation model. It works well for his dashboard. Marcus is not sure it works for anyone else. Can one data model serve every stage?

Marcus drafts a table with one row per stage: raw, cleaned, business, serving. Dev asks what goes wrong if the raw layer is a star schema. Each stage needs a model and an anti-pattern to avoid. Which goes where?

The payments team adds a column overnight and renames another, and three payment sources must merge into one cleaned layer. Lena asks whether Data Vault is worth the extra tables. When do hubs, links and satellites pay off?

A trip with two promos appears twice in Kofi's promo dashboard, inflating discount spend by 9%. His wide table cannot split it. Marcus sketches a bridge table. How should one trip be shared between two promos?

The cancellation model scores brilliantly offline and fails in production. Lena finds that training joined today's rider statistics onto old trips. Marcus asks her one question: what did the model actually know at request time?

A half-written trips table reaches the board dashboard for twenty minutes before the job finishes, and Kofi takes the questions. Grace says, "Nobody should ever see your work in progress." How do you publish only what passed?
teasers: Marcus drafts one table that gives every platform stage its own model.
Payments renames a column overnight, and three sources must become one.
Two promos on one trip inflate Kofi's discount numbers by 9%.
The cancellation model is brilliant offline and useless in production. Why?
A half-written table reaches the board dashboard, and Kofi takes the heat.
Next week: Asha wants one trip to travel the whole platform, end to end, by Friday.
modules.boss: Weekend review: the board saw half a trips table for twenty minutes. Marcus walks through the stage map, the model chosen for each layer and the write-audit-publish gate that would have kept broken data hidden.
modules.finale: Marcus walks Asha through every stage in forty-five minutes using a seven-step method. Kofi, quietly, backs the plan. Asha approves the map, then says, "Now show me one trip moving through all of it, by Friday."
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why school has a coat room and a lunch room. Marcus says, "Different rooms for different jobs, and our data needs different shapes for different jobs too."

modules.logline: Marcus builds the thinnest pipeline that runs end to end, from a ride event to a SQL answer, and learns why every step must survive a rerun.
scenes: Asha wants one ride event to travel from the app to a SQL answer by Friday. Marcus itches to perfect the Kafka layer first, and Dev bets he will not finish. Why build every layer badly before any layer well?

The old Hadoop cluster still holds three years of trips, and its NameNode has no standby. Dev refuses to touch it. Marcus must choose where new events land. What breaks if the NameNode dies, and what does object storage change?

Lena's Kafka consumer crashes, restarts, and forty trips are missing. She committed offsets before writing them. Marcus draws partitions and consumer groups on a napkin. Where should a consumer start after a crash?
Lena's first Spark job collects a day of trips to the driver to count them, and the driver runs out of memory. She almost hides it, then asks. Who should do the counting: the driver or the executors?
Dev shows Marcus forty Airflow DAGs with no owners, and one that has failed silently since March. Marcus writes the skeleton's first DAG with data intervals. What does a run for 09:00 actually cover?
Kofi asks how many trips Meridian did yesterday, and Marcus asks five questions back before writing any SQL. Then Lena reruns the 09:00 hour by hand after a fix. What happens when a job runs twice?
teasers: Dev refuses to touch a Hadoop cluster whose NameNode has no backup.
Lena's Kafka consumer crashes, restarts, and forty trips simply disappear.
Lena's first Spark job brings down the driver, and she almost hides it.
Dev opens forty Airflow DAGs with no owners, and one has failed since March.
Kofi asks a simple question, and Lena reruns an hour by hand.
Next week: Finance wants eighteen months of trips queryable in under ten seconds.
modules.boss: Weekend review: Bengaluru shows twice as many completed trips for the 09:00 hour as the app does, because a rerun appended instead of overwriting. Marcus must make every hop idempotent and explain it to Kofi.
modules.finale: One ride event travels from generator to Kafka, Spark, object storage and SQL, scheduled by Airflow, and a small LLM script explains failed runs to Dev. It is thin, but it walks. Then Finance tries an eighteen-month query.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why Marcus built something badly on purpose. He says, "I built a tiny version of every part first, so I know they all fit together."

modules.logline: Marcus moves raw trips from loose Parquet into an Iceberg table, and learns that every fast query is one that reads fewer bytes.
scenes: Finance's eighteen-month trips query takes four minutes, and Finance wants ten seconds. Dev suggests a bigger cluster. Marcus opens the query profile instead and sees most of the time spent reading. How do you read fewer bytes?

Raw trip events still land as JSON, eighty columns wide, and Finance reads five of them. Lena asks whether Parquet, Avro or ORC is best. Marcus says it depends on who writes and who reads. Which fits analytics?

Lena partitions the trips table by rider_id and creates four million directories. Listing them alone takes minutes. Marcus asks what Finance actually filters on. Which column makes a good partition, and when is bucketing better?

Yesterday's trips return zero rows on Kofi's dashboard. The files exist, but the Hive Metastore never registered the new partition. Kofi, for once, asks Marcus for help. Why does a Hive table trust directories nobody validates?

Marcus proposes Iceberg. Dev, sceptical of new tools, asks what it solves that Hive does not. Marcus draws snapshots, manifests and column ids on the whiteboard. Can a table really be a tree of metadata?

After a week of hourly writes, the Finance query has gone from two seconds to forty. The table now holds ten thousand tiny files. Grace says, "Every table needs a janitor." What should compaction run, and how often?
teasers: Lena asks which file format wins, and Marcus answers with a question.
One partitioning choice creates four million directories overnight.
Yesterday's trips vanish from Kofi's dashboard, though every file is still there.
Marcus proposes Iceberg, and Dev wants to know what it actually fixes.
A two-second Finance query now takes forty, and nobody changed the SQL.
Next week: festival season starts, and Bengaluru brings 80% of the trips.
modules.boss: Weekend review: the Finance query slowed twentyfold under ten thousand tiny files, and a renamed fare column turned a week of fares into NULLs. Marcus must explain compaction, Iceberg column ids and the DAG that keeps the table healthy.
modules.finale: Eighteen months of trips answer in under ten seconds, and Dev's maintenance DAG compacts the table every night. Failure alerts now arrive as structured fields, not prose. Then the nightly enrichment job warns: festival week starts Monday.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why Marcus tidied files all day. He says, "Finding one big book on a shelf is quicker than finding a thousand loose pages."

modules.logline: Festival week puts 80% of trips in Bengaluru, and Marcus learns to read a Spark job, find the skew and fix it without buying more machines.
scenes: Festival week starts, and the nightly enrichment job joining thirty days of trips to drivers and zones runs past breakfast. Tomas asks why the morning dashboard is empty. Marcus opens the Spark UI. Where does the time go?

Marcus reads the physical plan and sees the trip date filter applied after the join, not at the scan. Lena wrapped it in a Python UDF last month. What does Catalyst need before it can push a filter down?
The join stage writes 400 GB of shuffle for a 120 GB input. Dev asks why joining two tables moves so much data across the network. Marcus has to explain, step by step, what a shuffle really does.

The zones table has two hundred rows, yet Spark shuffles it alongside thirty days of trips. Drivers holds half a million rows. Lena suggests broadcasting both. Which join strategy fits each table, and why not both?

On the stage page, the median task finishes in eight seconds and one task runs for fifty minutes. It holds every Bengaluru trip, and Kofi's festival report waits on it. How do you split a key with 80% of the rows?

Adaptive query execution splits the skewed partition, but executors now spill to disk and one dies out of memory. Mei asks why the Spark bill doubled. Grace says, "Fix the data before you buy machines." How big should an executor be?
teasers: Marcus reads the plan and finds the date filter in the wrong place.
A 120 GB job writes 400 GB of shuffle, and Dev wants to know why.
A two-hundred-row table is being shuffled with thirty days of trips.
One task runs for fifty minutes. It holds every Bengaluru trip.
The skew is fixed, an executor dies anyway, and Mei arrives with the bill.
Next week: Finance's total for last Tuesday keeps changing, and nobody touched it.
modules.boss: Weekend review: on festival night the enrichment job went from twenty minutes to three hours, then failed at 40%. Bengaluru held 80% of the rows. Marcus must present three fixes, in order, with the evidence for each.
modules.finale: The job is back to twenty minutes in festival week, and Marcus's agent now reads plans and event logs to explain slow stages. Mei approves the smaller cluster. Then Finance's number for last Tuesday changes again.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why one checkout queue was so long. Marcus says, "Everyone from the biggest city stood in one line, so we opened more tills just for them."

modules.logline: Marcus and Kofi build a dbt warehouse on Snowflake that gives Operations and Finance the same answer, survives late data and earns the board's trust.
scenes: Operations says 412,000 trips yesterday. Finance says 398,500. Asha puts Marcus and Kofi in one room, and both show correct SQL. Kofi admits the word itself is the problem. What does completed actually mean at Meridian?

Lena finds 2,300 trips missing from the new star schema. Their driver_id is NULL, and the inner join drops them. Kofi asks whether the fact should just allow NULL keys. What should a dimension offer for unknown?

A driver moves from Pune to Bengaluru. Overnight, all his Pune trips from last year move to Bengaluru on the dashboard, and the city leads notice. Which slowly changing dimension type keeps history where it happened?

Kofi writes his first dbt model and asks Marcus to review it. They agree on staging, intermediate and marts folders, and Lena adds the tests. What should a dbt test catch before the board ever sees a number?

Finance's total for last Tuesday keeps changing. Trips completed at 23:58 arrive two days late, and the incremental filter never sees them. Lena proposes a lookback window. How many days, and what does it cost?

Tomas wants analysts to ask questions in plain English. The text-to-SQL bot answers confidently and wrongly, because completed still has two meanings. Grace says, "Teach the definitions before the machine." What must the agent see, and with which role?
teasers: Two thousand trips disappear from the star schema, and a NULL is to blame.
A driver moves city, and a year of his trips moves with him.
Kofi writes his first dbt model and asks Marcus to review it.
Finance's Tuesday total changes again. Some trips arrive two days late.
Tomas wants analysts to ask the warehouse questions in plain English.
Next season: Tomas wants everything real time, and the SQL bot meets the CEO.
modules.boss: Weekend review: a backfill meant to catch late trips double-counted a week of Finance revenue. Marcus and Kofi must show the merge on the trip key, the lookback window and why a rerun should change nothing it should not.
modules.finale: At the board meeting, completed and settled trips appear side by side, defined once in dbt, and both teams' numbers match. Kofi presents with Marcus. Lena's 2% gap stays in her notebook. Tomas smiles: "Now make it real time."
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why grown-ups argued about counting. Marcus says, "We used one word for two different things, so we gave each its own name, and now everyone agrees."

seasons.title: Real Time
seasons.logline: Tomas wants everything real time, and Marcus learns that fast data is only worth having when it is also correct, affordable and still standing when a region goes dark.

modules.logline: A text-to-SQL bot embarrasses the CEO, and Marcus learns that an answer is only as good as the meaning, permissions and scores behind it.
scenes: The board numbers finally match, and Tomas is already back with a new ask: a chat bot that answers any question from the warehouse. Marcus sketches the pieces on a whiteboard. Where does the model end and the data begin?

In Monday's leadership meeting, the CEO asks the bot for last week's Bengaluru revenue. It answers in four seconds, confidently, and double counts every split payment. The room goes quiet. How do you make generated SQL trustworthy?

Marcus reads the bot's query log. It joined trips to payments on the wrong key because "revenue" means three things in three tables. Kofi says the definitions already exist in dbt. Can the bot read them?
Lena notices the bot connects with a service account that can drop tables. Dev asks, flatly, who approved that. Marcus wants the bot to have tools, not passwords. What would an MCP server change?

Operations wants every rider complaint tagged by topic, forty thousand a week. Lena proposes a Python script that calls a model row by row. Marcus wonders whether the warehouse can do it in SQL. What does each row cost?

Asha agrees to a second demo on one condition: show her the score first. Marcus has fifty real questions from finance and no way to grade the answers. How do you evaluate a data agent before it meets the CEO again?
teasers: Tomorrow on Meridian: the CEO asks the bot a simple question, in front of everyone.
Tomorrow on Meridian: the query log shows exactly why "revenue" broke the bot.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Lena finds the bot's database account, and what it is allowed to drop.
Tomorrow on Meridian: forty thousand complaints a week, and nobody has time to read them.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Asha sets one condition for a second demo.
Tomorrow on Meridian: a driver sees two different wallet balances a minute apart.
modules.boss: Incident review: the CEO's double-counted revenue answer. Walk Asha through the guarded SQL, the semantic layer, the read-only tool and the eval score that would have caught it before the meeting.
modules.finale: The second demo scores 46 out of 50, and the bot says "I don't know" for the rest. Grace's advice: "Never ship an answer you cannot grade." That night, two Postgres replicas disagree about a driver's balance.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "Can your robot answer questions?" Marcus says: "Only if we teach it what our words mean and check its homework before anyone sees it."

modules.logline: A wallet bug turns into a split-brain incident, and Marcus goes back to how storage, replication and consensus really work.
scenes: Marcus volunteers for the wallet-balance postmortem and stalls on the first line. Why do payments live in Postgres while ride events sit in an LSM-based store? He realises he has never asked how either engine stores a row.
The timeline is clear now: the driver topped up on the primary, then read from a replica eleven seconds behind. Dev calls it normal. Marcus calls it a bug. Which reads must see their own writes?

Partitioning by city looked tidy until Bengaluru, with 80% of trips, landed on one shard. That shard runs hot every evening while thirteen others idle. How do you spread data without losing what belongs together?

Lena reproduces a rarer bug: two refunds approved for one order, both reading the same balance. Postgres was running read committed. Would a stricter isolation level have stopped it, and at what price?

Then the real incident surfaces. During a network blip, two database nodes each believed they were primary for ninety seconds and both accepted writes. How does a cluster agree on one leader, and whose clock wins?
As the fix rolls out, the driver dashboard's cache key expires and every request hits Postgres at once. The database falls over for four minutes. What should sit between users and the database?
teasers: Tomorrow on Meridian: an eleven-second gap explains the driver's two balances.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Bengaluru crushes one shard while thirteen others sit idle.
Tomorrow on Meridian: one order, two refunds, and the same balance read twice.
Tomorrow on Meridian: for ninety seconds, Meridian has two primaries.
Tomorrow on Meridian: a cache key expires and the database falls over.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Tomas wants surge prices per zone, updated every ten seconds.
modules.boss: Incident review: the split-brain wallet incident. Asha wants the full chain: replica lag, the isolation level, the failed leader election and the cache stampede that followed. Explain each layer as you would to an interviewer.
modules.finale: The postmortem ships with Dev's name beside Marcus's. Grace reads it over Friday coffee: "Every data tool is a storage engine with opinions." On Monday, Tomas arrives with a slide titled Surge Pricing, Live.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "Why did the app say two numbers?" Marcus says: "We keep copies of the notebook, and one copy was a few seconds behind."

modules.logline: Surge pricing moves onto Kafka and Spark streaming, and Marcus learns that data which never stops brings late events, duplicates and poison messages.
scenes: Tomas wants surge multipliers per zone, recalculated every ten seconds from live trip requests. The batch job runs hourly. Marcus lists what changes when data never stops: late events, no natural end. Why is streaming harder than batch?

Dev draws the trip-request topic: 48 partitions, keyed by zone. Lena asks why one consumer lags while the others idle. The answer is inside Kafka. How does it actually store, order and hand out messages?

In testing, a rider in Koramangala is charged surge twice for one request. The consumer crashed after writing but before committing its offset. At least once or exactly once: which guarantee does pricing really need?

Marcus rebuilds the surge job in Spark Structured Streaming with ten-second windows. Then a phone that lost signal uploads requests from twenty minutes ago. Should a late event change a price already shown?
The mobile team renames a field in the trip event without telling anyone. The streaming job keeps running, but surge in every zone drops to 1.0. How should a stream handle a schema that changes?
Friday, 11 p.m.: Nadia leaves for a night shift, Zoe is asleep, and Marcus is on call. The pager fires: one malformed message, consumer lag climbing past two million. Retry it, skip it, or park it?
teasers: Tomorrow on Meridian: one consumer drowns while its neighbours sit idle.
Tomorrow on Meridian: a rider pays surge twice for one ride.
Tomorrow on Meridian: twenty-minute-old requests arrive from a phone that lost signal.
Tomorrow on Meridian: someone renames a field, and surge drops to 1.0 everywhere.
Tomorrow on Meridian: a night shift, a sleeping child, and a pager that will not stop.
Tomorrow on Meridian: refunds in Postgres and the warehouse disagree, and Lena remembers the 2% gap.
modules.boss: Incident review: the poison message and the two-million-message lag. Dev wants the timeline, the dead-letter design, the guarantee pricing truly needs, and whether Flink, Spark or Kafka Streams should own surge next year.
modules.finale: Surge runs live in all fourteen cities, with a dead-letter topic and a lag alert. Nadia asks him to swap his next on-call week. Grace: "Choose the weakest guarantee the business can live with." Then finance flags mismatched refunds.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "What is a stream?" Marcus says: "A conveyor belt of little notes that never stops, so we add them up as they pass."

modules.logline: Refunds in Postgres and the warehouse disagree, and change data capture finally explains the 2% revenue gap from Marcus's first month.
scenes: Finance reports that October refunds in Postgres total more than refunds in Snowflake. Lena pulls up last year's month-end close: the same 2% revenue gap. The nightly export copies rows, but does it copy every change?

Marcus traces it: the export selects rows by updated_at, so refunds edited after the cut-off and rows deleted outright never arrive. Dev suggests reading the Postgres write-ahead log instead. How does log-based capture work?

Debezium now streams every change into Kafka. Each insert, update and delete must land in the Iceberg table once, in order. Lena asks what a delete even looks like in a lake. How do you apply changes to a table?
Kofi wants refunds on his dashboard within seconds. Marcus writes the same CDC job in Flink SQL, and it fits on one screen. But is shorter also correct when updates for one order arrive out of order?
The pipeline runs, and the totals still differ by 0.3%. Asha asks how anyone will know the numbers match tomorrow. Marcus needs a check that proves it every day. What do you count, and where?

The last causes are dull and real: refunds issued weeks after a trip, and a replication slot that once filled the disk. Lena proposes an agent that drafts the backfill. Who approves it before it runs?
teasers: Tomorrow on Meridian: the nightly export misses every change made after the cut-off.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Debezium arrives, and Lena asks what a delete looks like in a lake.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Kofi wants refunds in seconds, and Flink SQL makes it look easy.
Tomorrow on Meridian: the pipeline runs, and the totals are still 0.3% apart.
Tomorrow on Meridian: the last clue to the 2% gap is weeks old.
Tomorrow on Meridian: at 3 a.m., Lena cannot find the runbook that matters.
modules.boss: Incident review: the database and the warehouse disagree. Present the whole 2% story to Asha and finance: missed deletes, late refunds, the full slot, the CDC design and the daily reconciliation that now guards it.
modules.finale: For the first time since Marcus joined, the month closes with a difference of zero. Lena presents the fix herself. Grace: "Trust is a reconciliation you run every day." Then the on-call channel asks for help again.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "Did you find the lost money?" Marcus says: "It was never lost; we missed some changes, so now we write down every change as it happens."

modules.logline: On-call wants a bot that answers from runbooks, and Marcus treats retrieval as a data pipeline that must stay fresh, private and measured.
scenes: At 3 a.m. Lena is on call, the lag alert fires, and the fix sits in a runbook four pages deep in wiki search. Dev wants a bot that answers from runbooks. Marcus says it is a data pipeline first. Why?

The first prototype splits runbooks every 500 characters. Asked how to drain the dead-letter topic, it returns half a command and a heading from another page. How should documents be chunked and embedded?
Mei asks why the team needs a new vector database bill. Marcus checks whether Postgres with pgvector, or even DuckDB, could hold forty thousand chunks. Where should the vectors live?
Dev updates the CDC runbook after Tuesday's change, but a week later the bot still recommends the old command. On call, a stale answer is worse than none. How do you keep an index fresh?
Lena wants to load two years of postmortems too. Marcus finds rider phone numbers and driver names inside them. Can a model extract the useful parts as ETL without carrying personal data along?
Dev asks the question that matters: how often is the bot right? Marcus has anecdotes, not a number. How do you measure retrieval and answers separately, and when should the bot say it does not know?
teasers: Tomorrow on Meridian: the bot answers with half a command and the wrong heading.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Mei asks why forty thousand chunks need their own database.
Tomorrow on Meridian: the runbook changed last week, and the bot did not notice.
Tomorrow on Meridian: two years of postmortems, full of phone numbers.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Dev asks how often the bot is right, and wants a number.
Tomorrow on Meridian: the AI bill jumps fourfold, and the bot takes nine seconds to answer.
modules.boss: Incident review: the on-call bot that gave a stale command at 3 a.m. Show Dev the pipeline: chunking, the fresh index, redaction, citations, the abstain rule and the retrieval score that would have flagged it.
modules.finale: The runbook bot now cites its sources and abstains when unsure, and Lena's next shift ends early. Grace: "Measure retrieval before you touch the prompt." Then Mei forwards the model invoice with one word: why?
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "How does the robot know?" Marcus says: "It finds the right page in our instruction books first, reads it out, and says when it is not sure."

modules.logline: Model costs quadruple and answers slow to nine seconds, and Marcus puts a gateway, traces, evals and guardrails in front of every AI call.
scenes: The model bill is four times last month's, and the text-to-SQL bot now takes nine seconds to answer. Mei wants to know who pays. Marcus wants to know where the time goes. What changes once AI is in production?
Tracing one slow request, Marcus finds most of the nine seconds pass before the first token: a 30,000-token prompt stuffed with the whole schema. What is the model server doing while the user waits?

Mei builds a spreadsheet: input tokens, output tokens, retries, and three teams using the largest model for simple tagging. Every request has a price. Which changes make it cheaper and faster without making it worse?
Five teams call three model providers with five keys and no shared limits. One retry loop caused half the spike. Dev proposes a single LLM gateway in front of everything. What must the gateway own?

Lena moves the complaint tagger to a smaller model and costs drop 70%. Kofi asks whether the tags are still right. Nobody knows, because nothing scores answers in production. How do you keep score live?
A rider types a card number into the support bot, and it appears in a trace log. Asha wants guardrails before the next launch. Where in the request path do the checks belong?
teasers: Tomorrow on Meridian: a nine-second answer, and most of it before the first word.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Mei prices every request, and three teams look expensive.
Tomorrow on Meridian: five teams, three providers, five keys and one retry loop.
Tomorrow on Meridian: the cheaper model saves 70%, but are the answers still right?
Tomorrow on Meridian: a card number shows up in a log where it should not.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Asha signs off on the move to AWS, and Mei starts a new spreadsheet.
modules.boss: Incident review: the fourfold AI bill and the nine-second bot. Walk Mei and Asha through the traces, the cost per request, the gateway's limits and caching, the eval gate and the guardrails that close the gaps.
modules.finale: The bill falls below last quarter's and the bot answers in under two seconds. Grace: "Put a price on every request before anyone asks." Then Asha announces the data centre lease ends in March: Meridian moves to AWS.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "Why is the robot expensive?" Marcus says: "Every word it reads costs a little, so we taught it to read less and use a smaller brain for easy jobs."

modules.logline: Meridian moves its platform to AWS while Mei watches the bill triple, and launch night ends with a region going dark.
scenes: Asha gives the team one quarter to move the platform to AWS. Tomas asks whether streaming moves too. Marcus maps what changes and what stays the same: tables and jobs stay, storage, access and bills change. Where is the real risk?
Lena copies the lake to S3, and the first Spark job crawls, listing millions of tiny files. Dev asks about versioning and lifecycle rules. How does S3 really behave underneath the familiar paths?
Reviewing permissions, Marcus finds the Airflow role can read every bucket, payments included, through a wildcard. Nobody remembers why. How do you give each job only the access it needs in IAM?
Should the nightly batch run on EMR, Glue or containers on ECS, and who schedules it? Dev wants clusters he understands; Mei wants nothing running at 3 p.m. What decides the compute choice?
Two engineers click the same staging setup into existence by hand, and a job works in one and fails in the other. Marcus insists on Terraform. Can the whole batch path live as reviewed code?
Three weeks in, Mei posts the bill: triple the old data centre. Cross-zone transfer, idle clusters, a NAT gateway carrying every S3 read. Her question is short: who pays for this, and why?
teasers: Tomorrow on Meridian: the first Spark job on S3 spends its time listing files.
Tomorrow on Meridian: a wildcard role that can read the payments bucket.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Dev wants clusters, and Mei wants nothing running at 3 p.m.
Tomorrow on Meridian: two staging setups, built by hand, behave differently.
Tomorrow on Meridian: Mei posts the first full AWS bill, and it is triple.
Tomorrow on Meridian: season 4 begins, and Meridian is buying a company called Brightcart.
modules.boss: Incident review: the bill triples and a role is too broad. Show Mei and Asha the cost breakdown, the fixes for transfer and idle compute, the narrowed IAM roles and the Terraform that keeps them narrow.
modules.finale: Launch night: every pipeline runs on AWS and the dashboards are green. Grace texts: "Test the failover before you need it." At 1:40 a.m. the pager fires. A whole region is dark, and surge has stopped.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "What is the cloud?" Marcus says: "A huge computer room we rent by the minute, so we must remember to switch the lights off."

seasons.title: The Merger
seasons.logline: Meridian buys Brightcart, and Marcus must merge two platforms, two teams and two ways of working while Brightcart's architect, Viktor Hale, competes for the same job.

modules.logline: Marcus inherits Brightcart's Scala, JVM and Kubernetes estate and must learn to read it before he can judge it.
scenes: Launch night ends at 4 a.m.: traffic fails over to the second region and Lena closes the incident. At nine, Asha announces Meridian is buying Brightcart. Viktor Hale's estate runs on the JVM. Why should a Python engineer care?

Viktor shares a repository and says nothing. Marcus opens it: case classes, Options, pattern matches, a for-comprehension over Futures. Lena says it looks like Python wearing armour. Can Marcus read Scala well enough to review it by Friday?

Brightcart's nightly fare job is a Spark Scala pipeline of typed Datasets and a few UDFs. Viktor calls it faster than anything Meridian runs. Marcus spots a map over every row. Is it really faster, or just harder to read?

At 2 a.m. the Brightcart fare job dies with an OutOfMemoryError. Lena, now leading on-call, pages Marcus. The executor heap looks fine, yet the container was killed anyway. Two kinds of out-of-memory, one alert. Which one is this?

Brightcart runs Spark and Flink for forty teams on one shared Kubernetes cluster. Pods sit Pending all morning while one team's job hogs the nodes. Viktor shrugs: requests and limits are the teams' problem. Are they, on a platform?

In a corner of Brightcart's estate sits a Hadoop cluster: YARN queues, Hive tables, eight years of ride history. Viktor wants it gone in a quarter. Dev wants it left alone. What does a safe migration off Hadoop look like?
teasers: Viktor sends Marcus a Scala repository with no comment and a Friday deadline.
Brightcart's fare job runs in Scala, and Viktor says Python could never keep up.
A 2 a.m. page: the JVM runs out of memory, but not where anyone looks.
Forty teams, one Kubernetes cluster, and pods that will not schedule.
Hidden in Brightcart's estate: a Hadoop cluster holding eight years of ride history.
Brightcart runs Databricks, Meridian runs Snowflake, and the board wants one set of tables.
modules.boss: Saturday's review: the Brightcart fare job that died at 2 a.m. Viktor blames Meridian's data volume; Marcus suspects off-heap memory. Lena chairs. Read the Scala, the GC logs and the pod events, then decide who is right.
modules.finale: Marcus approves Viktor's pull request with three comments, all correct. Viktor replies with one word: fair. Grace says, 'Learn their stack before you judge it.' Then finance asks why the same trips table exists twice, in Databricks and Snowflake.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What did you build today?" Marcus: "Nothing new; I learned to read another team's language so I can help the people who wrote in it."

modules.logline: Brightcart's Databricks and Meridian's Snowflake must serve one set of tables, and one rider's deletion request tests whether either can.
scenes: Merger day thirty. Brightcart's analysts live in Databricks notebooks; Meridian's finance team lives in Snowflake. Mei finds both platforms storing the same trips and billing for both. Tomas asks why there are two. Is either team wrong?

Viktor walks Marcus through a Delta table: Parquet files, a _delta_log of JSON commits, a checkpoint every ten. One query scans four thousand tiny files. How does Delta decide which files to skip, and why is it skipping so few?

Marcus returns the favour in Snowflake: micro-partitions, clustering, a warehouse that suspends after sixty seconds. Viktor's query runs in eight seconds here, but bills credits by the second. Which engine prunes better, and which is cheaper per answer?

Asha wants one copy of trips, readable from both engines. Viktor proposes Delta with UniForm; Marcus suggests Iceberg tables that Snowflake can read. Both plans dodge the same question. Who owns the writes when two engines share one table?

A rider in Bengaluru emails support: delete my data, everywhere. Her trips live in Delta, in Snowflake and in three old snapshots. Legal gives thirty days. Deleting a row is easy. How does Marcus prove it is gone from history too?

Brightcart tags support tickets with a language model inside a nightly batch job. It is cheap until a failure makes it retry every row. Viktor wants it in Snowflake next. Should a model sit inside a pipeline, and on which platform?
teasers: Viktor opens a Delta table's log and shows Marcus how it really works.
Marcus answers with Snowflake micro-partitions and the same query, timed on both.
Asha wants one copy of the trips table, read by two engines.
A rider asks to be deleted from everywhere, and legal starts a thirty-day clock.
A language model in a batch pipeline bills for every retry, row by row.
Overnight, 12% of Brightcart's trip rows disappear, and every job shows green.
modules.boss: The weekend review: the rider deletion. Support says it is done; an auditor finds her trips in a Delta time-travel version and a Snowflake clone. Walk through vacuum, retention, clones and masking, and show where the process leaked.
modules.finale: One trips table, two engines, and a deletion runbook legal signs. Viktor admits Snowflake's pruning surprised him. Grace says, 'Two tools is fine; two truths is not.' Then on Monday the trip count drops 12% overnight.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why do you need two computers to hold the same toys?" Marcus: "We don't; we are teaching both of them to share one toy box."

modules.logline: When 12% of rows vanish without a single failed job, Marcus and Lena build tests, contracts and write-audit-publish so failures can no longer hide.
scenes: Monday standup. Every Airflow task is green, yet the Brightcart trips table holds 12% fewer rows than on Friday. Tomas's dashboard already shows a dip in Chennai demand. Nothing failed. How does a pipeline lose data while reporting success?

Lena traces the loss to an inner join against a driver table that arrived late. No test checked row counts. Viktor says Brightcart tests in production. Marcus asks which tests would have caught this, and where they should run.

The driver table belongs to a Brightcart partner team, who renamed a column last Thursday without telling anyone. Viktor calls it their right. Marcus calls it a broken promise. What would a data contract between the teams actually say?

Dev proposes a rule: no table is published until it is audited. Viktor worries it doubles storage and slows every job. Marcus sketches write, audit, publish on a staging branch. Can bad data wait there without consumers noticing the delay?

Asha asks for one health dashboard: freshness, volume, schema and distribution. Lena adds CI that runs the tests on every pull request. Then a harmless rename passes CI and breaks a Snowflake view. What did the checks not see?

At 3 a.m. Lena runs an incident herself, calm, with a clear timeline in Slack. Afterwards she asks Marcus for an on-call agent that reads Airflow failures and gathers evidence. How much should an agent diagnose before a human looks?
teasers: Lena finds the missing rows behind a join that nobody tested.
A partner team renamed a column last Thursday and told nobody.
Dev wants no table published until it passes an audit.
A health dashboard stays green while a Snowflake view quietly breaks.
Lena leads a 3 a.m. incident alone, then asks for an agent.
Asha asks Marcus to design for ten times the traffic, and a lost region.
modules.boss: The weekend review: 12% of rows vanished and nobody was paged. Lena presents the timeline. Find the root cause, the missing contract, the test that should exist, and where write-audit-publish would have stopped the bad load.
modules.finale: The contract is signed, the audit step blocks bad loads, and Lena's postmortem is the clearest Marcus has read. Viktor copies it for Brightcart. Grace says, 'Make the failure loud before you make it rare.' Then Asha books a design review.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "How do you know all the toys are there?" Marcus: "We count them before anyone plays, and if some are missing, the box stays shut."

modules.logline: Asha asks for a design that survives ten times the traffic and a lost region, and Marcus and Viktor must design it out loud together.
scenes: Asha books a design review: the combined company expects ten times the trips within two years. Marcus and Viktor each get forty-five minutes at the whiteboard. Viktor starts drawing at once. Marcus starts with questions. Which approach does the room trust?

Marcus does the arithmetic aloud: two hundred million events a day, about two thousand a second, peaks ten times higher on festival nights. Mei asks what a year of storage costs. Do his numbers hold up under her questions?

The rider app needs a trip's fare in under fifty milliseconds. Viktor proposes reading straight from Delta. Dev suggests a key-value store. Kofi wants Snowflake. Three serving stores, one latency budget. Which one fits the access pattern?

Viktor asks what happens when two regions accept the same payment update. Marcus reaches for quorum, idempotency keys and exactly-once. Lena asks which of those words actually stops a double charge. Can Marcus explain it plainly?

Asha calls a surprise drill: the primary region is gone, now. Traffic doubles elsewhere, Kafka lag climbs, warehouse loads stall. Marcus and Viktor share one whiteboard and ten minutes. What fails first, and what do they shed?

Lena brings a pipeline an AI assistant wrote for the drill: tidy, documented, and wrong in two places. Viktor finds one, Marcus the other. What mistakes does AI-written pipeline code make, and how should a reviewer hunt for them?
teasers: Marcus estimates ten times scale aloud, and Mei asks what a year costs.
Three teams, three serving stores, and a fifty-millisecond budget for one fare.
Two regions accept the same payment, and Lena wants plain words.
Asha switches off a region mid-review and starts a ten-minute clock.
An AI-written pipeline looks perfect, and is wrong in two places.
Viktor proposes that every Brightcart domain team owns its own data, and Kofi objects.
modules.boss: The weekend round: the lost-region drill, replayed. Ten times the traffic, one region dark, Kafka lag rising. Clarify, estimate, draw, go deep, break it and scale it, in forty-five minutes, as Marcus and Viktor did.
modules.finale: The drill ends with no lost payments and a one-page design both names sign. Asha calls it the first document from the merged team. Grace says, 'Draw the failure first.' Then Viktor sends a memo proposing data mesh for everyone.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What if the big computer room loses power?" Marcus: "Another room in another city takes over, and we practise that before it ever happens."

modules.logline: Viktor's push for data mesh forces Marcus to decide which domains should own their data products and which still need a central team.
scenes: Viktor's memo lands in every inbox: dissolve the central data team and give each domain its own data. Kofi's analysts worry. Dev calls it a reorganisation dressed as architecture. Why does data mesh exist, and what problem does it solve?

Asha asks for one example before any reorganisation. Marcus picks the trips dataset: an owner, a contract, SLOs, a catalogue entry, a stable interface. Lena asks what makes it a product rather than a table with a nice name.

The payments domain refuses: two engineers, no data skills, a quarter-end audit coming. Viktor says ownership is non-negotiable. Marcus suspects mesh is the wrong answer for some teams. How does he decide which domains are ready?

If every domain builds its own pipelines, who runs storage, access and quality checks? Marcus sketches a self-serve platform; Viktor adds policies enforced as code. Dev asks who wins when a domain's rule conflicts with the central one.

The trips product launches. Three weeks later, two teams use it and five still query the old warehouse copy. Kofi will not switch until it matches his numbers. How do you move consumers off a central warehouse without breaking them?

Viktor shows Brightcart's earlier mesh attempt: forty data products, eleven owners who have left, nine with no consumers. He wants it done properly this time. Marcus asks which failure modes companies hit, and which ones they are already repeating.
teasers: Asha wants one real data product before anyone reorganises anything.
The payments team refuses to own their data, and Viktor will not budge.
Domains want independence, and Dev wants to know who sets the rules.
The new trips product is live, and Kofi still queries the old copy.
Viktor opens Brightcart's graveyard of forty abandoned data products.
Dev's new pipeline template has been live six weeks, and no team uses it.
modules.boss: The weekend review: Viktor's mesh proposal, as Asha will hear it on Monday. Name which domains own data products, write one product spec with an owner, a contract and an SLO, and say where mesh is the wrong answer.
modules.finale: Three domains own products; payments stays central for now. Viktor calls it half a mesh. Marcus calls it the half that works. Grace says, 'Move ownership only where someone wants it.' Then Dev's new template sits unused.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Who owns the toys?" Marcus: "Whoever plays with them most looks after them, and promises to keep them tidy for everyone else."

modules.logline: Dev's pipeline templates sit unused until Marcus and Viktor learn to build golden paths that teams choose rather than obey.
scenes: Dev's pipeline template has been live six weeks with zero users. Brightcart teams copy Viktor's old Scala scaffold instead. Dev wants to mandate the template. Marcus wants to know why nobody chose it. What is a golden path, really?

Marcus lists how teams actually ship: a new batch pipeline, a data product, a backfill, a stream. Lena times each one: eleven days for a new pipeline. Viktor says pave everything. Which journey should they pave first?

Lena drafts the template: Airflow DAG, dbt models, tests, owner tag, alerts and cost labels, all on by default. Viktor asks how a team escapes when it needs something different. What belongs in a template, and what stays optional?

Two months later, thirty pipelines built from the template run three different versions of it. A security fix reaches only nine. Dev sighs that templates always rot. How do you keep a template alive after teams copy it?

Kofi's team wants to skip platform review, which takes a week. Viktor proposes a developer portal with one-click creation. Marcus proposes CI checks instead of the review meeting. Can guardrails replace a gate without letting risk through?

Asha asks whether the golden path works. Dev shows downloads. Marcus shows time to first pipeline, down from eleven days to one. Viktor shows the teams that left it. Which number proves teams actually chose the road?
teasers: Lena times how long a new pipeline really takes: eleven days.
The first template ships, and Viktor asks where the exit is.
Thirty pipelines, three template versions, and a security fix that reaches nine.
Kofi wants to skip the weekly platform review, and Marcus agrees with him.
Asha asks for one number that proves the golden path works.
A dashboard shows rider phone numbers to four hundred people who never needed them.
modules.boss: The weekend review: nobody uses our templates. Decide which journey to pave, what the template sets by default, how it stays current, which checks move into CI, and which metric shows teams chose it.
modules.finale: Nine of twelve new pipelines now start from the path, and Viktor's team ships one too. Grace says, 'Make the right way the easy way.' Then Lena finds rider phone numbers in a dashboard four hundred people can open.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why don't people just do it your way?" Marcus: "Because we made our way the easiest one, so now most of them want to."

modules.logline: Rider phone numbers in an open dashboard push Marcus to build governance that protects riders without slowing the teams that need the data.
scenes: Four hundred people can see rider phone numbers in a Brightcart dashboard. Nobody has misused them. Legal wants every dashboard locked. Kofi says locking everything stops the business. What is governance for, if not for saying no?

Marcus asks how many columns hold personal data. Nobody knows: names, emails, drop-off coordinates, a free-text notes field. Viktor suggests tagging by hand. Lena counts eleven thousand columns. Can classification run automatically, and how accurate must it be?

Support needs a rider's phone number for an open ticket, in their own city only. Roles alone would mean forty new roles. Viktor proposes attributes and row rules. How do roles, attributes and policies combine without becoming unmanageable?

Data scientists need to join trips to riders without seeing who the riders are. Masking breaks the join; Viktor suggests tokenisation; legal asks about pseudonymisation. Three words that sound alike. Which one protects riders and keeps the join?

A column tagged personal in Snowflake loses its tag after one Delta transform. Meanwhile legal puts a hold on Chennai trips that retention rules want deleted. Which rule wins, and how does lineage carry a tag downstream?

The auditors arrive on Monday and ask for evidence: who accessed rider data, under which policy, approved by whom. Viktor's team keeps policies in a wiki. Marcus keeps them in code. Which one survives an audit?
teasers: Lena counts eleven thousand columns, and nobody knows which hold personal data.
Support needs one phone number, and roles alone would need forty new roles.
Data scientists need to join riders to trips without knowing who they are.
A personal-data tag vanishes after one transform, and legal places a hold.
The auditors arrive on Monday, and Brightcart's access policies live in a wiki.
Asha asks a simple question nobody can answer: what does the platform team do?
modules.boss: The weekend review: the phone-number dashboard. Show how the column escaped classification, which policy should have masked it, how lineage would have carried the tag, and what evidence you would hand the auditors.
modules.finale: The audit closes with no findings, and teams barely notice the new rules. Viktor moves Brightcart's wiki into code without being asked. Grace says, 'Good governance is the kind people forget is there.' Then Asha asks what the platform is for.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why can't everyone see everything?" Marcus: "Some things are private, like your diary, so only people who really need them get the key."

modules.logline: Running the merged platform as a product puts Marcus and Viktor side by side on service levels, cost and adoption, until Asha must choose one of them to lead it.
scenes: Asha merges both teams into one data platform and gives Marcus and Viktor a quarter to prove it is worth funding. Tomas asks what the platform team actually does. Neither has a crisp answer. Who are its users, really?

Marcus proposes SLOs: trips fresh by 6 a.m. on 99.5% of days. Viktor wants 99.9%. Lena asks what happens when the error budget runs out in week two. Does the team stop shipping features, or keep going?

A Snowflake outage hits during the finance close. Lena runs the incident well, but forty teams learn of it from Kofi. Viktor says the fix mattered more than the updates. How should a platform team communicate during an incident?

Mei brings the bill: the merged platform costs more than both did apart, and nobody knows which team spends what. She wants showback by Friday. Viktor fears it starts a turf war. What is the right unit cost for a trip?
